name: Italy
governanceModel: First EU member state with its own comprehensive national AI law

First-mover national AI law vs. EU harmonisation
overview:
Italy became the first EU member state to pass its own comprehensive national AI law, Law No. 132/2025, which entered into force in October 2025 and layers sector-specific rules — for healthcare, employment, justice and the professions — plus new AI copyright provisions on top of the EU AI Act baseline. Implementing decrees are due by October 2026; two received preliminary Council of Ministers approval in June 2026, with final adoption still pending parliamentary committee and Data Protection Authority (Garante) review.

Undersecretary Alessio Butti has framed the law as a 'digital sovereignty' matter, citing a reported €1 billion national AI investment figure that has not been independently corroborated beyond his own public statements. The law's copyright provisions add new AI-specific text-and-data-mining exceptions and require substantial human creative contribution for AI-assisted works to receive copyright protection; legal commentators note that the precise boundary of the TDM exception — in particular whether it extends to commercial model training or is limited to research/non-commercial use — remains contested and not yet fully settled in practice.

currentDirection.summary: Italy moved first among EU states to legislate its own comprehensive national AI law rather than rely on the EU AI Act alone, and is now working through implementing decrees — due by October 2026 — that will help determine how strictly its national copyright and sector rules end up being enforced. Two decrees have preliminary Council of Ministers approval but still require parliamentary committee and Data Protection Authority review.

recentDevelopments.text: Two implementing decrees for Italy's national AI law received preliminary Council of Ministers approval (covering national authorities/education/training, and policing/civil and criminal liability); final adoption remains pending parliamentary committee and Data Protection Authority (Garante) review ahead of the October 2026 deadline.
Undersecretary Alessio Butti cites a reported €1 billion national AI investment, framing it as a matter of digital sovereignty.
UNU signs agreements with the Italian government to establish a new AI and big-data institute in Bologna; as of mid-2026, parliamentary ratification and full operational status were still pending.

debates.topic: TDM copyright restriction scope contested by industry vs. rightsholders
debates.summary: Italy's national law narrows text-and-data-mining exceptions for AI training compared with the EU baseline, and is generally regarded by legal commentators as stricter — though the precise boundary between permitted research/non-commercial use and commercial model training remains contested and, per some analyses, ambiguous.
debates.expanded: Some AI developers and legal commentators argue that a narrower TDM exception could make Italy a harder jurisdiction to train commercial models in compared to peers relying solely on the EU AI Act's copyright framework, though the exact scope of the exception is still being debated and may only be clarified through future guidance or litigation. Rightsholders and creative-industry groups have broadly welcomed a stricter default, arguing it better protects Italian creative and publishing industries.

debates.topic: First-mover national AI law vs. EU harmonisation
debates.summary: As the first EU state with its own comprehensive AI law, Italy tests whether national add-ons atop the AI Act help or fragment the single market.
debates.expanded: The European Commission has generally pushed for harmonised AI Act implementation across member states; Italy's decision to legislate additional sector-specific and copyright rules raises the question of whether other states will follow suit (creating a patchwork within the EU itself) or whether Brussels will push back on national divergence.
